paras: The lynching of Bragg Williams took place at Hillsboro, Texas, on January 20, 1919, when a mob took Williams, a Black man under sentence of death, from the Hill County jail and burned him on the public square. He had been convicted of murdering Mrs. George Wells and her child near Itasca, and the mob formed after his attorneys gave notice of appeal. Because he had already been sentenced, Black editors cited the burning against the claim that lynching answered the failure of the courts.

Mrs. Wells and her child were found murdered near Itasca on December 2, 1918, and Williams was arrested that day and "spirited away to avoid threatened violence." In early January the Dallas Express reported him held in the Dallas County jail for safekeeping after mob threats, giving the charge as an assault on a woman. Convicted the week before January 20, he was sentenced that morning by Judge Horton Porter, and his appointed attorneys, refused a new trial, gave notice of appeal.

According to the wire report, the appeal "enraged residents of the Itasca neighborhood" and a mob was organized. County officers attempted to control the crowd, but it battered in the jail door with a telephone pole, rushed the guards and seized Williams. In the Wisconsin Weekly Blade's version, the mob was admitted "after a short parley with the officers."

About one o'clock Williams was taken to the public square, tied to a post and burned on an oil-soaked pyre of boxes and barrels. Between 300 and 400 people, including dozens of women, watched; the body was consumed in about forty minutes, and the crowd, called "orderly," dispersed quietly.

On January 21 the NAACP telegraphed Dallas demanding the arrest and punishment of the mob. The governor denounced the burning, according to the Houston Post. An NAACP meeting reported in the Dallas Express named a committee to memorialize the governor, and a Calvert correspondent wrote that the mob had "stirred the minds of all the Colored people in Texas."

In March an Austin dispatch reported that the Hill County grand jury had returned no indictments. Attorney General Cureton then asked the court of criminal appeals to cite mob members for contempt, arguing that the notice of appeal had put the case under its jurisdiction, a step the dispatch called unprecedented in Texas. No report of an inquest or of the application's outcome appears in the coverage.

Black papers ran a Hillsboro wire dispatch in late January under headlines from the Black Dispatch's "Negro Is Burned in Texas" to the Richmond Planet's "Brutal Texas Mob Burns Man Convicted of Double Slaying." The Wisconsin Weekly Blade headed its account "Another Lynching" and wrote of the mob's "shouts of glee."

Editorials turned on the prior conviction: the Richmond Planet wrote that authorities "took no drastic steps" and urged raising the case at the Peace Conference, and the Blade asked "which committed the worse crime." The Bookertee Searchlight wrote of the "hyaenas at Hillsboro," and the New York Age said white lynchers had already "monopolized" Bolshevist methods.

White Texas opinion reached Black readers secondhand, through reprinted Dallas News and Houston Post editorials condemning the burning and a New York Times editorial on the Post's call for federal action. The case recurred through July in a Washington Bee list, a Tulsa Star letter, a Houston Informer editorial and a Richmond Planet chronology of burnings.

The Baltimore Afro-American said prejudice ruled the trial, that Williams was not allowed to testify and that a frame-up was alleged. Against the wire's "orderly" crowd, it reported that businesses and schools were closed to swell the crowd and that officers were present but did not resist.
Reports also differed on the hanging date (February 21, 12 or 20), and one Dallas Express dispatch alone said Williams "confessed."

reader.title: Lynching of Bragg Williams
bases: A mob took a Black prisoner under death sentence from the Hill County jail and burned him on the public square (A3, A8, A15).

A mob of several hundred broke into the jail and burned Williams to death without lawful authority (A3, A6, A15), acting on his conviction for murder after his attorneys gave notice of appeal (A3, A9).

The wire report (A3, A8, A15) and independent accounts in the Wisconsin Weekly Blade (A2) and Baltimore Afro-American (A18) agree that a mob seized Williams from the Hillsboro jail and burned him; they differ only on details.

accounts.label: Houston Post (reprinted)
accounts.gist: The burning was among the most atrocious in recent Texas history and was denounced by the governor.

framing.detail: Wire text with headlines from 'Negro Is Burned in Texas' to 'Brutal Texas Mob Burns Man Convicted of Double Slaying'.
Editorials (Richmond Planet, Wisconsin Weekly Blade, Bookertee Searchlight, Houston Informer) stress he was already sentenced and call the mob 'hyaenas' and 'hill-billies and roughhouses'.
The Afro-American disputes the wire's 'orderly' crowd and questions the fairness of the trial.
